title: Catastrophic Krakatau eruption and tsunami sequence, August 1883
summary: The 1883 Krakatau eruption culminated in catastrophic explosions and caldera collapse on 26–27 August, destroying much of the pre-1883 island and generating destructive tsunamis along Java and Sumatra. More than 36,000 fatalities are commonly reported, with most attributed to tsunamis. The event also produced globally recorded atmospheric-pressure effects. LEGEND separates direct tsunami propagation from remote water-level disturbances that NOAA notes may have been excited by atmospheric gravity waves.

time.note: The catastrophic phase is modeled as 26–27 August 1883; precursor activity began earlier in 1883.

historicity.note: The eruption, collapse, tsunamis, and widespread observations are extensively documented. Confidence does not imply every historical measurement or casualty estimate is exact.

uncertainty: Historical casualty totals vary by source and counting method; the canonical record preserves the widely cited >36,000 scale rather than claiming an exact universal total.
Not every remote water-level disturbance recorded globally should be interpreted as a direct ocean-traveling tsunami.
alternative_interpretations: For some distant tide-gauge disturbances, NOAA identifies atmospheric gravity-wave coupling as a plausible explanation where direct tsunami propagation was blocked by continents.

review.note: Canonical scope covers the eruption-collapse-tsunami sequence and explicitly separates nearby direct tsunami impact from some remote atmosphere-coupled water-level signals.
